pages.text: Many molecules come in two mirror-image forms, like hands. Living things use only one: the wrong hand of a drug can be useless, or a poison. A $(thing)chiral catalyst$() lowers the barrier to one hand by ΔΔG‡ more than to the other, so that one forms $(thing)s = e^(ΔΔG‡/RT)$() times faster; the enantiomeric excess is ee = (s − 1)/(s + 1).

The $(item)Chiral Ligand$() is made at the Synthesis Bench with the Ouroboros's $(item)Kekule Ring$() in its catalyst slot (the ring never wears). In the $(item)Asymmetric Reactor$()'s catalyst slot it makes $(item)Enantiopure Reagent$() from Fine Reagent and hydrogen. Run it cold enough for ee ≥ 0.9: colder is purer, and slower.

Two routes, by choice: the reactor is $(thing)fast but random$() (60% of runs give the reagent); the Chromatography Column $(thing)resolves$() two Fine Reagents into one, slowly, every time - it separates the two hands and throws one away.
